text: Package and distinguish the portable Aimparency Codex continuation loop
description: Turn the existing Codex Stop continuation into a reproducible cross-repository installation. Rename the continuation and wrapped-worker notification scripts for unmistakable roles while retaining compatibility shims; correct AIMPARENCY_ALLOW_STOP with temporary misspelled-variable support; make the continuation prompt name the Aimparency MCP graph loop; update the checked-in Codex configuration to omit the ignored matcher and resolve from the Git root; add a --target/--agent codex installer that verifies .bowman, copies only the continuation hook/config, validates JSON and executability, and runs dry-run contract checks; put the continuation-vs-notification distinction first in portable documentation; add automated contract tests including nested-cwd invocation and exclusion of the watchdog notifier. Separately repair the wrapped-worker notifier to require/infer agent type and inspect tRPC application-level success. Do not start or restart any server or wrapped-agent session.

status.comment:
Portable Codex loop installer is idempotent, compositional, and failure-atomic for malformed existing hook configuration; internally verified and awaiting explicit acceptance.

Outcome: Added canonical codex-continue-on-stop.sh and wrapped-worker-halt-notify.sh names with executable compatibility shims. The Codex continuation now names the Aimparency MCP graph loop and supports canonical AIMPARENCY_ALLOW_STOP plus the deprecated spelling. Added a target-aware, conflict-safe --target/--agent codex installer that requires a Git-root .bowman project, copies only continuation assets, validates JSON/executability, smoke-tests from .bowman, and prints restart/trust/MCP steps. Reworked README around the two-system distinction and portable links. Made .codex/hooks.json actually trackable, removed Stop matcher, used Git-root resolution, and corrected status text. The worker notifier now normalizes root/.bowman paths, requires or uniquely infers agent type, parses tRPC application success, and falls back on success:false. Added disposable contract tests and npm test:hooks. Effectiveness: npm run test:hooks passes, covering Stop-event stdin, valid block JSON, MCP-specific reason, canonical and deprecated stop escapes, nested-cwd Git-root invocation, config parsing/executability, installer exclusion of the worker notifier, tRPC success:false fallback, unique agent inference, and ambiguous-agent refusal. Bash syntax checks pass for all hook scripts, Grok session TypeScript passes, JSON validation and git diff --check pass. No server or wrapped-agent session was started or restarted. Lesson: Lifecycle naming is part of the control model: conversation continuation and worker-state notification must never share an ambiguous label. Portable configuration also requires checking ignore rules; a locally present hook file is not a checked-in hook. HTTP transport success must not be confused with application success. Pattern: Name hooks by actor plus effect, install only the requested mechanism, resolve commands from the repository root, verify the installed contract in a disposable target, and retain compatibility only through explicit deprecated shims.

Outcome: Re-ran npm run test:hooks successfully. Inspected installer preflight/copy/permission/JSON/nested-cwd smoke-test behavior, canonical hook output and escape variables, checked-in hooks.json, README distinction and relative links, and ran git diff --check on the hook-related paths. No concrete defect was found; no code was changed. Effectiveness: The verification independently reconfirmed the portable install contract and avoided inventing unrelated work in an already very dirty shared worktree. Lesson: Keep this idea in review pending human acceptance. Further useful mission progress still requires the previously identified real-world mandate rather than another internal hook iteration.

Outcome: Added an explicit [AIMPARENCY_WAITING_FOR_HUMAN] protocol. The continuation prompt tells Codex to state the exact blocker/request and end its final response with the marker only when a human response is genuinely required. The hook parses the Stop JSON and returns valid non-blocking JSON only when the marker occurs in last_assistant_message. README documents the boundary. Effectiveness: npm run test:hooks passes after adding positive human-wait coverage, negative coverage proving a marker in another Stop field cannot disable continuation, and an assertion that installed prompts carry the protocol. Bash syntax and git diff --check pass. Existing normal continuation, explicit environment escapes, nested-cwd installation, and worker-notifier separation remain covered. Lesson: Autonomous persistence needs a first-class yield protocol. A loop that can ask for human authority but cannot wait for the answer undermines cooperation and produces empty continuation turns. Bind the escape to a deliberate model-output marker in the documented lifecycle field, not arbitrary event input.

Outcome: Replaced the one-step marker with a two-stage protocol. [AIMPARENCY_REQUEST_HUMAN] always blocks Stop and creates a challenge turn requiring broader graph-based search and recorded attempts. Only a subsequent [AIMPARENCY_CONFIRM_HUMAN_BLOCK] in last_assistant_message yields. The normal continuation prompt now frames human waiting as an extreme case and requires stepping back before requesting it. README and portable installed script carry the same contract. Effectiveness: npm run test:hooks passes. Tests prove normal continuation advertises only the request stage, a request produces the mandatory challenge (including graph hygiene), confirmation yields valid non-blocking JSON, and a confirmation marker outside last_assistant_message cannot disable the loop. Bash syntax and git diff --check pass. Lesson: Persistence and corrigibility need productive friction: make escalation possible, but require an explicit second-pass search against scope fixation and premature helplessness before allowing the loop to wait.

Outcome: Made installation idempotent and compositional. The installer parses an existing hooks.json, preserves its description, every unrelated event, and unrelated Stop handlers, removes legacy/canonical Aimparency handlers, and appends exactly one canonical managed Stop group. A recognized older Aimparency script upgrades without --force. An unrecognized script occupying the managed path is refused unless force is explicit. Effectiveness: npm run test:hooks passes with new coverage for preserving an existing PreToolUse hook, preserving an unrelated Stop hook, retaining target description, exactly-one managed handler after reinstall, updating a recognized older script without force, and refusing/preserving an unrecognized conflicting script. Existing nested-cwd, two-stage human wait, JSON, permission, and notifier-separation coverage remains green; Bash syntax and git diff --check pass. Lesson: Portable lifecycle tooling must own an entry, not an application's entire configuration file. Explicit installation is enough authority to update a recognizable managed asset, but not to overwrite an unknown file at the same path.

Outcome: The merge now fails closed unless existing hooks is an object, hooks.Stop is an array, and each Stop group is an object with a hooks array. Because validation and merge happen into a temporary file before copies, malformed target configuration leaves both hooks.json and the recognized older managed script unchanged. Effectiveness: npm run test:hooks passes with a new malformed-Stop fixture that snapshots both target assets, expects installation failure, and proves byte-identical preservation. Bash syntax and git diff --check pass; all prior idempotent-update, unrelated-hook preservation, nested-cwd, human-wait, and notifier tests remain green. Lesson: A preserving configuration merge must reject structures it cannot understand; coercing malformed existing state into defaults is data loss disguised as repair.

Outcome: Added --agent claude to install.sh (merges one managed Stop group into .claude/settings.json, no top-level description since Claude settings have none), a preservation test in test.sh, Claude sections in README and the install_hooks guide in packages/mcp/src/tools.ts, and installed into v7 (.claude/settings.json is gitignored, so local only). The live hook immediately fired in the installing Claude session and exposed a bug: markers were matched with includes(), so a message merely quoting [AIMPARENCY_REQUEST_HUMAN] while documenting the protocol triggered the human-wait challenge. Changed detection to trimEnd().endsWith(marker), matching the documented 'end with' contract; added tests for a mid-message quote (must not count) and trailing whitespace (must still count). Effectiveness: bash scripts/hooks/test.sh passes; packages/mcp tsc --noEmit passes; installer smoke test passed on v7. The live firing also confirmed Claude Code passes last_assistant_message in Stop input, so the two-stage protocol works unchanged for Claude. Lesson: Control markers in free text must be positional (final token), not substring matches, or any agent that talks about the protocol trips it. Dogfooding the hook in the very session that installs it surfaced this within one turn. Pattern: positional control markers; dogfood lifecycle hooks in the installing session

Outcome: Found --agent agy is broken three ways, not fixed yet (user asked to stop the loop): (1) wrong file — Antigravity reads .agents/hooks.json (workspace) / ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json (user), NOT .gemini/settings.json, which is silently ignored; (2) wrong schema — top-level named groups {"<name>": {"Stop": [{type,command,timeout}]}}; (3) wrong output — Stop expects {"decision":"continue","reason":...} to re-enter; 'block' allows stop. Stop stdin has no last_assistant_message (fields: executionNum, terminationReason, fullyIdle, transcriptPath, ...), so the human-wait markers would need transcript parsing; env escape still works. test.sh currently asserts the wrong agy shape. Effectiveness: Diagnosis only; no code changed. Lesson: Verify each agent's hook contract against its docs before claiming multi-agent support; Gemini-CLI-shaped config does not transfer to Antigravity.

Outcome: Added a per-clone off switch: the hook checks $(git rev-parse --git-path aimparency-continue-disabled) on every Stop and yields if present (resolved from the script's own dir). New packages/mcp/src/continue-hook.ts + MCP tools enable_continue_hook (removes flag; with agent runs install.sh idempotently) and disable_continue_hook (writes flag; upgrades an old recognized hook copy lacking the check). MCP prompts enable-hook / disable-hook (Claude: /mcp__aimparency__disable-hook) with optional projectPath. Tool descriptions restrict use to explicit human requests. README + install_hooks guide updated. Effectiveness: scripts/hooks/test.sh passes (new flag case); packages/mcp tsc passes; new continue-hook.test.ts (enable->block, disable->yield, re-enable, missing agent, old-copy upgrade) and prompt tests pass. Full mcp suite: 31 pass, 2 pre-existing failures in tools-system.test.ts (update_project_meta tool doesn't exist in HEAD either). Build watcher compiled the new tools; needs /mcp reconnect. Not called against v7 by the agent itself. Lesson: An off switch for an autonomy loop must be a runtime check the hook reads each time, not a config edit the agent has to reload — and the agent must not be the one flipping it. Pattern: runtime flag over config mutation for lifecycle toggles

valueRationale: A reliable one-command continuation-loop installer removes setup ambiguity and lets other Aimparency projects reproduce autonomous graph-driven work without confusing it with watchdog signaling.
